title: Miles Davis: Kind of Revolution
description: Cool jazz and restless innovation—one legendary recording era.

questions.question: Which trumpeter handed his band only sketches—no rehearsals—for the sessions that became 'Kind of Blue'?
questions.explanation: "I wanted a lot of spontaneity in the playing," he wrote in his autobiography. It paid off: the album was certified 5× platinum in the U.S. in 2019, 60 years on.

questions.question: In what year was Miles Davis's 'Kind of Blue' recorded?
questions.explanation: Two sessions, March 2 and April 22, in Columbia's 30th Street Studio, a converted church in Manhattan. Side one came from day one; side two, seven weeks later.

questions.question: On the 1959 'Kind of Blue' sessions, which tenor saxophonist played alongside Miles?
questions.explanation: Cannonball Adderley played alto beside him. Two weeks after the final session, Trane cut 'Giant Steps'—a blizzard of chord changes, the polar opposite of what Miles wanted here.

questions.question: Coltrane joined Miles in what new approach—improvising over scales instead of chord changes—on 'Kind of Blue'?
questions.explanation: On 'So What,' the band rides one Dorian scale for 16 bars, slides up a half step for the 8-bar bridge, then comes home. Pianist Bill Evans helped shape the sound—and wrote the liner notes.

questions.question: Bill Evans's liner notes claimed those modal jazz pieces were each captured in how many complete takes?
questions.explanation: Nearly true: 'Flamenco Sketches' took two. The real twist? A tape machine ran slow on day one, so side one played about a quarter-tone sharp for 33 years, until engineers caught it in 1992.
